summary: Describes the set of Microsoft vendor-specific RADIUS attributes, which carry extra information between network access servers and authentication servers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a computer asks to join a network, a gatekeeper can pass notes about it. This lists the special note types Microsoft added.

questions: what are microsoft vendor specific radius attributes
subtitle: A public reference list of the extra RADIUS attributes Microsoft remote access products use for passwords, encryption keys and dial-up settings.

tldr.problem: The standard RADIUS attribute set does not cover Microsoft's own dial-up protocols and features, so third parties had no open reference for interoperating with Microsoft products.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of sub-attributes carried inside the RADIUS Vendor-Specific attribute with Vendor-ID 311. They cover MS-CHAP versions 1 and 2, MPPE encryption keys, bandwidth allocation (BAP), ARAP and miscellaneous items such as DNS server addresses.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It was meant to be updated whenever Microsoft defines a new vendor-specific attribute.

today: RFC 2548 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a reference list of these attributes, not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Microsoft Attributes Exist
sections.content:
RFC 2548 describes the set of Microsoft vendor-specific RADIUS attributes. They support Microsoft proprietary dial-up protocols, or add features that the standard RADIUS attribute set (RFC 2138) does not provide.

The stated purpose is an open, easily accessible reference for third parties who want to interoperate with Microsoft products. The memo expects to be updated whenever Microsoft defines a new vendor-specific attribute. It states that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.plainLanguage: Microsoft made some new kinds of notes for its own dial-in system. This paper writes them all down so other companies can read the same notes.

sections.title: Packing Sub-attributes into One Attribute
sections.content:
Each Microsoft attribute is a sub-attribute carried inside a RADIUS attribute of type Vendor-Specific. The Vendor-ID of the outer attribute MUST be set to decimal 311 (Microsoft).

More than one sub-attribute MAY share a single Vendor-Specific attribute. They SHOULD then be packed as Vendor-Type, Vendor-Length and Value triples after the initial Type, Length and Vendor-ID fields. The Length field of the outer attribute MUST equal the sum of the sub-attributes' Vendor-Length fields plus six.

Section 3 of the RFC adds a table showing which attributes may appear in which packet types (Access-Request, Access-Accept, Access-Reject, Access-Challenge and Accounting-Request) and how many times.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a big envelope with Microsoft's name on it. Inside, you can slip several small notes, and each note says how long it is.

sections.title: MS-CHAP Version 1 and 2 Attributes
sections.content:
Microsoft's CHAP dialect, MS-CHAP, is negotiated with CHAP Algorithm 0x80 (version 1) or 0x81 (version 2) in LCP option 3. The attributes mirror its differences from standard CHAP.

For version 1, the NAS sends MS-CHAP-Challenge (type 11) and the client answers with MS-CHAP-Response (type 1, length 52). That response holds an LM-Response and an NT-Response, each 24 octets. If the Flags field is one, the NT-Response is preferred. MS-CHAP-Domain (type 10) names the Windows NT domain, and MS-CHAP-Error (type 2) carries failure text in Access-Reject packets.

For version 2, which adds mutual authentication, MS-CHAP2-Response (type 25) carries a 16-octet Peer-Challenge and a 24-octet Response. MS-CHAP2-Success (type 26) returns a 42-octet authenticator response string in Access-Accept packets.

Password changes after expiry use further attributes: MS-CHAP-CPW-1 and MS-CHAP-CPW-2, MS-CHAP2-CPW, and the MS-CHAP-LM-Enc-PW and MS-CHAP-NT-Enc-PW attributes. The encrypted password is 516 octets, too long for one RADIUS attribute, so it is split into pieces with a 2-octet sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a secret handshake at a clubhouse door. The guard asks a question, you answer in a way only a real member can, and there are special notes for changing your secret word.

sections.title: MPPE Keys and Encryption Policy
sections.content:
Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption (MPPE) encrypts PPP packets with RC4 and supports 40-bit and 128-bit session keys. Several attributes carry its settings, all in Access-Accept packets.

MS-CHAP-MPPE-Keys (type 12, length 34) holds an 8-octet LM-Key and a 16-octet NT-Key, padded and encrypted like the User-Password attribute. MS-MPPE-Send-Key (type 16) and MS-MPPE-Recv-Key (type 17) each carry one key, for packets sent to or received from the remote host. Each has a 2-octet Salt whose leftmost bit MUST be set, and its contents MUST be unique within the packet. The String is padded to a multiple of 16 octets and encrypted in blocks using MD5 over the shared secret, the Request Authenticator and the Salt.

MS-MPPE-Encryption-Policy (type 7) is 1 for Encryption-Allowed or 2 for Encryption-Required. MS-MPPE-Encryption-Types (type 8) has an L bit for 40-bit RC4 and an S bit for 128-bit RC4.
sections.plainLanguage: When you are let in, the gatekeeper hands over a lock key in a sealed, scrambled note. Another note says whether using a lock is optional or a must, and how strong it can be.

sections.title: BAP, ARAP and Miscellaneous Attributes
sections.content:
Three attributes control the PPP Bandwidth Allocation Protocol (BAP) for multilink calls. MS-BAP-Usage (type 13) is 0 for not allowed, 1 for allowed and 2 for required. MS-Link-Utilization-Threshold (type 14) gives a percentage from 1 to 100 below which a link may be dropped. MS-Link-Drop-Time-Limit (type 15) gives the seconds a link must stay under-utilized before it is dropped.

Four attributes support the Apple Remote Access Protocol (ARAP): MS-Old-ARAP-Password (19), MS-New-ARAP-Password (20), MS-ARAP-Password-Change-Reason (21) and MS-ARAP-Challenge (33).

Miscellaneous attributes include MS-RAS-Vendor (9) and MS-RAS-Version (18) to identify the RADIUS client, MS-Filter (22) for traffic filters, MS-Acct-Auth-Type (23) and MS-Acct-EAP-Type (24) for accounting, and the primary and secondary DNS (28, 29) and NetBIOS name server (30, 31) addresses for the PPP peer.
sections.plainLanguage: There are also notes for how many phone lines a caller may use, for Apple computers, and for telling the caller where the address book servers are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MS-CHAP, like PPP CHAP, is susceptible to dictionary attacks, so passwords should be chosen with care and be long enough to deter easy guessing.

The scheme protecting the Keys field of MS-CHAP-MPPE-Keys, MS-MPPE-Send-Key and MS-MPPE-Recv-Key is believed to be relatively secure on the wire. However, RADIUS proxies decrypt and re-encrypt the field when forwarding. These attributes therefore SHOULD NOT be used on networks where untrusted RADIUS proxies reside.
sections.plainLanguage: A short, easy password can be guessed, so pick a long one. And do not pass your lock key through a messenger you do not trust, because the messenger opens it on the way.

items.label: MS-CHAP-Challenge
items.desc: Challenge sent by the NAS to an MS-CHAP user.

items.label: MS-CHAP-Response
items.desc: Version 1 response with LM and NT parts.

items.label: MS-CHAP-Domain
items.desc: Windows NT domain of the authenticated user.

items.label: MS-CHAP-Error
items.desc: Error data, only in Access-Reject packets.

items.label: MS-CHAP2-Response
items.desc: Version 2 response with a peer challenge.

items.label: MS-MPPE-Send-Key
items.desc: Key for packets sent from the NAS to the remote host.

items.label: MS-MPPE-Recv-Key
items.desc: Key for packets the NAS receives from the remote host.

items.label: MS-MPPE-Encryption-Types
items.desc: L bit for 40-bit RC4, S bit for 128-bit RC4.
